item.title: Characterizing ENSO Teleconnections Impact on Gross Primary Productivity across CMIP6 Earth System Models
item.dc:creator: Maria Salazar, Gretchen Keppel‐Aleks, Allison L. Steiner
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: sea surface temperature, Earth system model, Earth system, CMIP, ensemble
Abstract The El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is the dominant mode of interannual variability in the climate system, altering global circulation patterns and causing changes in temperature and precipitation in remote regions through teleconnections. Because ecosystems are sensitive to climate variations, ENSO teleconnections have large implications for the magnitude of carbon uptake by terrestrial vegetation at interannual timescales. Using ten CMIP6 Earth System Models during 1950–2014, we find global carbon uptake is reduced 0.68± 0.18 PgC per °C increase in the Nino3.4 sea surface temperature, primarily due to reduced gross primary productivity (GPP), with a secondary contribution from increased heterotrophic respiration. We quantify the ENSO impact on GPP and identify several key regions in the tropics (Amazon, Southeast Asia) and extratropics (Australia, Northwest North America) where the ensemble shows regionally coherent, statistically significant changes to GPP. In the Amazon, most models suppress GPP due to increased temperature, but three models exhibit a weaker reduction or slight enhancement in GPP. Inter-model differences in background soil moisture state mediate the relative importance of temperature compared to radiation in controlling total and ENSO-driven GPP variability in the Amazon, with drier models exhibiting a stronger temperature-driven response and tending to exhibit greater reductions in GPP associated with ENSO. Our results suggest that, across the ensemble, land model sensitivities to simulated physical climate anomalies play a large role in the GPP response to ENSO conditions and that these responses differ regionally even within the same latitude range.

item.title: Isotope-based age scale with multi-month precision for the SE-Dome II ice core from Southeast Greenland over the past 150 years
item.dc:creator: Saaya Hamamoto, Yoshinori Iizuka, Takuro Aizawa, Kaoru Kawakami, Mai Matsumoto, Sumito Matoba, … (+6)
item.description:
Climate of the Past — matched: Greenland, Arctic, ice core
We developed a new 150-year age scale for an ice core from southeast Greenland by matching its oxygen-isotope variations with climate-model simulations. The record resolves changes over several months and shows that snowfall remained nearly evenly distributed through the seasons from 1871 to 2020. This stability suggests that the regional balance of atmospheric circulation and moisture transport changed little at this site despite recent Arctic warming.

item.description:

Preprint under review for ESSD (discussion: open, 0 comments) Antarctica is changing, but long-term coastal observations remain rare. This study brings together more than 30 years of data from Potter Cove, Antarctica, including seawater temperature, salt content, microscopic plant pigments, and suspended particles. item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: reanalysis, remote sensing, heat wave
This research presents a high-resolution ocean reanalysis dataset for the South China Sea covering 2001 to 2024. The dataset assimilates satellite remote sensing data and in-situ observations. It provides daily mean three-dimensional fields of temperature, salinity, currents, and sea surface height. Validation results show good agreement with observations. The dataset has been used to support studies of marine heatwaves, mesoscale eddies, and related processes in this important region.

item.title: GPU-accelerated atmospheric chemical kinetics using single precision in the ECHAM/MESSy (EMAC) model v2.55 with MEDINA v2.0
item.dc:creator: Kyriacos Sophocleous, Timo Kirfel, Domenico Taraborrelli, Theodoros Christoudias
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: Earth system model, Earth system
We address a major bottleneck in Earth system models, the high computational cost of simulating atmospheric chemical reactions, using graphics processing units. The MEDINA code-to-code compiler supports switching from double-precision to single-precision arithmetic on the accelerator, reducing average processing times by 30 %. Tests showed that this more efficient approach maintains high accuracy, with results matching traditional methods within 0.004 %.

item.title: The ocean–atmosphere turbulent flux algorithm in E3SMv2 does not always converge to unique and physical solutions: analysis and potential remedy
item.dc:creator: Justin Dong, Michael A. Brunke, Xubin Zeng, Carol S. Woodward, Hui Wan, Christopher J. Vogl
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development — matched: Earth system model, Earth system
Accurately computing ocean–atmosphere turbulent fluxes, which measure the transfer of momentum, heat, and water between the Earth and its oceans, in Earth system models is important for overall model accuracy. Under certain meteorological conditions, the set of equations utilized in many Earth system models to parameterize these fluxes can have no solution or more than one solution. Modifying the equations to address these issues leads to substantial changes to the simulated turbulent fluxes.

item.title: Learning Calibrated and Samplable Predictive Distributions of Surface-Ocean $\Delta p$CO$_2$ Using Tabular Diffusion Models
item.dc:creator: Gabriele Accarino, Mohammad M. Amirian, Thea H. Heimdal, Amanda R. Fay, Galen A. McKinley, Viviana Acquaviva
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: uncertainty quantification, ensemble, machine learning
arXiv:2611.21769v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The ocean absorbs almost 30% of anthropogenic CO$_2$ emissions, but quantifying this sink requires estimating surface-ocean CO$_2$ from observations that are sparse in space and time. Most existing machine-learning estimates of this field are deterministic, giving a single value per grid point, with uncertainty approximated post hoc via residuals, ensembles, or prescribed distributions. We instead learn a conditional predictive distribution for each observation: using Treeffuser, a conditional diffusion model with gradient-boosted-tree score functions, we estimate the full predictive distribution of $\Delta p$CO$_2$ (the sea-air $p$CO$_2$ difference) from 13 environmental, spatial, and temporal predictors. On a held-out SOCAT test set, Treeffuser attains the lowest continuous ranked probability score among the uncertainty-quantification methods evaluated (8.229 $\mu$atm) and the coverage closest to the nominal 68% / 95% levels (0.686 / 0.930), while retaining point-prediction skill comparable to a deterministic XGBoost baseline (RMSE 18.4 vs. 17.7 $\mu$atm; $R^2$ 0.77 vs. 0.79). These results show that conditional diffusion can provide well-calibrated, observation-level uncertainties while largely preserving point-prediction skill. Because Treeffuser is generative, its samples can support probabilistic analyses of $\Delta p$CO$_2$; extending this to spatially coherent field reconstruction will require modeling dependence across grid cells and evaluation on spatially held-out data.

item.title: A regime dependent parameterization of the refractive-index structure parameter $C_n^2$
item.dc:creator: Yal\c{c}{\i}n Ata, Muhsin Caner G\"ok\c{c}e, Yahya Baykal
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: parameterization
arXiv:2611.22641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vertical profiles of the refractive-index (RI) structure parameter, $C_n^2$, are required in atmospheric-optics calculations. The Hufnagel--Valley (HV) model is a useful reference profile and it is widely used however, it is difficult to say that it produces consistent results at the observed altitude, magnitude, and thickness of all turbulent layers and it can diverge from realistic measurements in particular height ranges, sites, and stability regimes. This study develops a regime-dependent RI structure parameter considering meteorological conditions and, more importantly, it provides a structure that can be calibrated against measured $C_n^2$ throughout the surface layer (SL), atmospheric boundary layer (ABL), and free atmosphere. The formulation combines SL including distinct unstable, near-neutral, and stable limits; convective ABL; and free-atmospheric turbulence when kinetic-energy and temperature-variance dissipation rates are available. The $C_n^2$ is formed by weighting the contribution of different layers. We use representative, physically plausible meteorological profiles to examine the model's limiting behavior, transitions between atmospheric regimes, continuity, sensitivity to its parameters, and propagation-related differences from the HV 5/7 model. The intended outcome is a measurement-calibrated model that remains physically interpretable across meteorological regimes.

item.title: Global gridded air-sea oxygen flux inferred from a machine learning-based dissolved oxygen product
item.dc:creator: Yuming Jin, Britton B. Stephens, Eric J. Morgan, Manfredi Manizza, Jonathan Sharp
item.description:
Earth System Science Data — matched: machine learning
We produce monthly air-sea O2 flux estimates (2004-2024) on a 1°×1° grid using machine learning-based dissolved oxygen fields (GOBAI-O2, Sharp et al., 2023). Fluxes are calculated with multiple gas exchange schemes and wind products, then constrained to match independent regional to global annual mean flux estimates. We evaluate flux seasonal cycles and annual patterns against atmospheric O2 observations and quantify flux uncertainties from multiple sources.

item.title: Bridging the knowledge gaps: A global mapping of capacity building offerings on climate change and health
item.dc:creator: Jaafar Tfayli, Sara Kassab, Zahraa Chamseddine, Shadi Saleh, Nour El Arnaout
item.description:
PLOS Climate — matched: climate change
by Jaafar Tfayli, Sara Kassab, Zahraa Chamseddine, Shadi Saleh, Nour El Arnaout Climate change is an escalating global health threat with disproportionate effects in climate-vulnerable regions. Building capacity at the intersection of climate and health is essential to equip healthcare systems and professionals to assess risks and sustain resilient services. This study maps online publicly accessible capacity-building offerings on climate change and health, focusing on accessibility and applicability to the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region. A rapid web mapping review identified courses, non-accredited certificates, accredited certificates, and diplomas offered by universities and institutions, excluding master's and PhD programs. Learning outcomes/objectives and metadata (provider type, geography, modality, language, credentialing) were extracted and thematically coded to characterize targeted domains. Twenty-two offerings were identified. Most were courses 82% (n = 18), followed by non-accredited certificates 9% (n = 2), accredited certificates 4.5% (n = 1), and diplomas 4.5% (n = 1). Providers included academic institutions 50% (n = 11), international organizations 27% (n = 6), and e-learning platforms 23% (n = 5). Delivery was predominantly online, 77% (n = 17), with some hybrid, 23% (n = 5) (Fig 2A). Nearly all offerings were in English, 96% (n = 21), with one multilingual; none were in Arabic. Provider geography was largely global (n = 13) or based in the United States (n = 6), with isolated entries from Germany (n = 1), Australia (n = 1), and Kenya (n = 1). No offerings originated from the MENA region. Thematically, programs emphasized climate Change and health policy, governance, leadership, and health impacts, while equity, resilience, competency alignment, applied operations, and stackable credentialing were minimally addressed. Overall, the landscape remains fragmented and rooted in the global north. Key gaps include co-designed, practice-oriented training with climate-vulnerable regions, especially MENA, embedding clear competencies, authentic assessment, and multilingual accessibility.

item.title: Projection of global daily CO2 emissions in 2026
item.dc:creator: Tao Li, Zhu Deng, Philippe Ciais, Steve J. Davis, Ling Ye, Zhu Liu
item.description:
arXiv physics.ao-ph — matched: CO2
arXiv:2611.22406v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Global fossil-fuel combustion and industrial-process CO2 emissions remain close to historical highs, yet the recent slowdown in growth is difficult to assess before conventional inventories become available. We project emissions for 2026 and examine daily departures during major climate and energy disruptions. Carbon Monitor activity-based estimates from 1 January 2019 to 30 September 2026 are combined with Prophet projections for 1 October to 31 December across 47 region-sector series. Global emissions are estimated at 38.1 Gt CO2 in 2026, 36.6 Mt CO2 (+0.10%) above 2025. The reference 68% range for the year-on-year rate is +0.011% to +0.18%. Five September-cutoff hindcasts show lower daily forecast errors for Prophet than for a seasonal-naive benchmark. Regional increases total 0.32 Gt and decreases total 0.29 Gt, so 94.0% of the 0.61 Gt gross movement cancels in the global sum. China contributes the largest reduction (-0.19 Gt), concentrated in industry and ground transport, whereas India contributes the largest increase (+0.19 Gt), led by power and industry. Heat-period power anomalies differ among countries and can be muted by summer averaging, while aviation and shipping show different disruption and recovery profiles. Resolving the near-zero global change reveals where reductions are concentrated and where continued growth offsets them, providing a timely basis for assessing the breadth of mitigation progress.

item.title: Evaluation of precipitation variability over complex terrain based on observations and high resolution WRF v4.2.2 modelling
item.dc:creator: Emilio Greciano-Zamorano, J. Fidel González-Rouco, Jorge Navarro-Montesinos, Cristina Vegas-Cañas, Félix García-Pereira, Elena García-Bustamante, … (+9)
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
This study compares observed and simulated rainfall in a mountainous area in central Spain from 1991 to 2020. It uses data from high and low elevations, along with long-term simulations and tests at very fine detail. While the finest detail tends to overestimate rainy days, it better captures heavy rainfall events. Overall, the results improve understanding of rainfall patterns and the benefits of higher detail.

item.title: The stippled grid points are statistically significant: (mis)uses of false discovery rate correction for geospatial data
item.dc:creator: Michael Konrad Schutte, Leonardo Olivetti, Flavio Maria Emanuele Pons, Gabriele Messori
item.description:
Geoscientific Model Development
When testing whether signals on maps are statistically meaningful, scientists must account for multiple testing. Otherwise, some results may appear significant purely by chance. We show that the widely used Benjamini–Hochberg correction can be misleading: simply changing the geographic region analyzed can make the same data appear far more statistically significant, even though nothing has changed. We recommend transparent reporting and using region-wide averages instead of pointwise testing.
